The paper by Lii and Lee (2012) has the highest total link strength in this cluster (36). The conceptual model proposed by the authors in this paper examines the effectiveness of three corporate social responsibility activities – cause-related marketing, sponsorship, and philanthropy on consumer–company identity, brand attitude, and, as a result, consumer behavior. In the same vein, Gupta and Pirsch (2006) investigate the relationship between the firm, the cause, and the customer and how the fit between these three groups affects consumer response. Cui et al. (2003) examine the CaRM concept on generation Y respondents. Moreover, Polonsky and Wood (2001) explore the negative consequences associated with CaRM and how to reduce them. Other papers in this cluster examine the framework for understanding CaRM programs (Brønn & Vrioni, 2001; Pirsch et al., 2007; Till & Nowak, 2000).

This cluster originally included 8 papers, one of which is deleted (Arora & Henderson, 2007) because it discussed embedded premium. The article by Grau and Folse (2007) in this cluster has the highest citations (234) and the link strength of 21. In this paper, the authors investigate the impact of donation proximity and message framing on customers’ campaign attitudes and participation intentions. The paper by Vanhamme et al. (2012) has the highest link strength in this cluster (26). The authors propose and test a comprehensive model of the influence of different cause attributes involved in cause-related marketing campaigns on corporate image. Robinson et al. (2012) demonstrate that those campaigns will get greater customer support in which customers themselves choose the cause that should be supported. The paper by Berger et al. (2006) focuses on examining CaRM to define organizations to their members. Other three papers (Chang, 2008; Koschate-Fischer et al., 2012; Winterich & Barone, 2011) have studied the CaRM by employing the donation attributes in their studies.

Cluster 3 also comprises 8 papers. This cluster mostly contains highly cited articles. The paper by M. Barone et al. (2000) has received the maximum number of citations in this cluster (487). The paper directly addresses the issue of consumers favoring the companies that use CaRM campaigns. In the same context, Nan and Heo (2007) also examine consumers’ attitudes toward the company by studying the role of brand cause fit in CaRM. The other papers measure the consumers’ perception of the CaRM strategies adopted by the 288 P. K. PANDEY AND N. BAJPAI retailers (M. J. Barone et al., 2007) and consumers’ responses to corporates implementing CaRM (Cornwell & Coote, 2005; Dean, 2003). The other two papers use brand equity (Hoeffler & Keller, 2002) and brand fit (Zdravkovic et al., 2010) to evaluate consumer responses to CaRM initiatives.

This cluster contains 4 articles. The paper by Pracejus and Olsen (2004) has received the maximum citations in this cluster (249) and also the secondhighest link strength (11). Using conjoint analysis, this paper describes the role of fit between brand and cause on choice when the cause is well-liked. Additionally, Folse et al. (2010) investigate the impact of donation amounts and purchase situations on customer perceptions and CaRM involvement intentions. The other paper in the cluster by (Elving, 2013) focuses on the role of firm reputation and the fit between the company and the CSR domain on skepticism, purchase intentions, and attitude toward companies. The paper by Pracejus et al. (2003) describes the role of advertising copy formats that describes the campaigns and how the customers interpret these. It can be concluded that cluster 4 is a group of articles discussing the role of different factors in the effectiveness of CaRM.

Cluster 5 is the smallest cluster among all the clusters, with only 3 articles. This cluster contains the studies, with the first author being Lafferty B.A. In this cluster, Lafferty et al. (2004) not only received the maximum citations (250) but also has the maximum link strength (29). In this paper, the authors develop a model that explains the impact of previous attitudes toward the cause and the brand on the alliance and the new attitudes developed toward both parties as a result of the alliance. In his study, Lafferty (2007) explains that the fit between cause and brand does not always play a key role in attitude formation and purchase intentions. For a better attitude toward the cause, (Lafferty & Goldsmith, 2005) suggests that when a cause is unfamiliar, associating it with a well-known brand increases attitudes toward the cause. All the articles are related to cause and brand, indicating a strong relationship among the articles in this cluster.
